status: DRAFT — domain check of every definition pending (SPEC/35 §8 item 2). Definitions explain the word, never the situation (§1).
formSyntax: A form is one or more words separated by spaces. In a word, a leading or trailing * stands for any further letters (an ending, the first part of a compound), a # for one or more digits; a form starting with = matches case-sensitively. A form always covers whole words.

terms.definition: The fastest-moving part of a fire, usually on its downwind side. Flames are normally highest at the head.
A side edge of a fire, between the head and the heel. A flank is usually named by its direction, e.g. the south flank.
The rearmost edge of a fire, on its upwind side. It usually spreads the slowest.
A continuous, advancing edge of a fire. The word is also used for the part of a fire advancing in one direction, e.g. the south-east front.
The whole outer boundary of the burnt area. Perimeter mapping means measuring that boundary, e.g. with a drone.
An edge of a fire is contained (under control) when its spread has been stopped, e.g. by an extinguished line. An uncontained edge can still move.
The place where the fire started.
A fire spreading in nature: in a forest, a bog, a meadow or a field.
A fire spreading in the ground layer (moss, shrubs, litter, bushes). The tree crowns do not burn.
A fire that has risen into the tree crowns and spreads from crown to crown. It is fast and hot.
A single tree catches fire from the trunk to the top, like a torch.
A glowing piece of bark or needles carried by the wind. An ember can start a new fire outside the fire's edge.
A small, separate fire outside the edge of the main fire, usually started by an ember.
Slow burning without flames, e.g. in peat, stumps or moss. A smouldering spot can smoke for a long time.
A spot thought to be out or quiet bursts into flames again, usually after smouldering.
A place hotter than its surroundings, usually found with a thermal camera. It can be a smouldering or burning spot not visible to the naked eye.
Organic soil built up from plant remains in a bog. Dry peat can burn and smoulder deep in the ground for a long time.
A bog in which ditches have been dug to dry it, e.g. for forestry. Dried-out peat burns more easily than a wet bog.
Fallen needles, leaves, twigs and dead plants on the ground. Dry litter catches fire easily.
The top layer of the forest floor above the mineral soil: moss, litter and decaying plant matter. When it is dry, fire can also spread in it below the surface.
A long, narrow ridge of sand and gravel left by the Ice Age. Eskers are dry and often covered in pine forest.
How strongly a fire burns, i.e. how much heat its edge gives off. An intensity class is a scale on which a higher number means higher flames.
How fast the fire's edge moves, often in metres per minute (m/min).
A short moment when the wind is stronger than usual. Wind is often reported as the mean wind and its gusts.
The water vapour in the air as a percentage of the most the air could hold. In dry air, plants dry out and catch fire more easily.
The temperature at which the moisture in the air starts to condense into water. The further the air temperature is above the dew point, the drier the air.
A computed estimate of where the fire's edge may be after a given time. It is a model's estimate, not an observation.
A unit of area: 1 ha = 10,000 m², e.g. 100 m × 100 m.
Fire hoses joined into one line that carries water from a pump or a vehicle to where it is used.
A hose fitting that splits one hose into two or more branches.
The device at the end of a hose that sprays the water. It sets the shape of the spray and the amount of water.
A portable engine-driven pump that takes water straight from a lake, river or pond into a hose line.
A hose line fitted with sprinklers that spray water. It wets a strip of ground.
A folding water tank set up in the field. A tanker fills the basin, and a pump takes the water from it.
A place where firefighting water can be taken, e.g. a lake, a river, a pond or a hydrant.
Carrying water with a tanker from a water point to where it is used and back. One round is filling, driving, emptying and returning.
A farm trailer tank for spreading slurry, pulled by a tractor. At a wildfire it can carry water.
A strip from which burnable material has been removed (trees felled, soil scraped or wetted) so that a fire cannot cross it.
The start of a firefighting line is tied to a place that cannot burn, such as a road, water or burnt ground, so that the fire cannot get round the line's start.
A fire lit on purpose from a control line, such as a road edge, towards an approaching fire. It burns away the fuel between the line and the fire before the fire arrives.
A way of fighting fire in which water or hand tools are applied directly to the burning edge.
A line chosen ahead of the fire, e.g. along a road or water, at which its spread is to be stopped. The line is prepared and strengthened before the fire reaches it.
Keeping an existing line, such as a road, water or a cleared strip, so that the fire does not cross it. The line is watched and wetted, and spot fires that start beyond it are put out.
Work in which units protect buildings and people, e.g. by wetting the ground around the buildings.
Work in which smouldering and hot spots in the burnt area are put out so that the fire does not start again.
A watch that goes round the burnt area after the fire is put out, looking for spots that start again.
A route agreed in advance along which a crew can quickly reach safety if the fire threatens.
A place where a crew is safe from the fire, e.g. already burnt ground, a field or a shore.
A person who watches the fire and warns the crew if the situation changes.
A sign or distance agreed in advance: when it is reached, the crew acts as agreed, for example withdraws. It is set so that there is still time to act before the danger arrives.
A safety memory aid for wildfire work: Lookouts, Awareness, Communications, Escape routes and Safety zones.
An overhead line carrying electricity. 20 kV (kilovolts) is a common voltage of the rural distribution network.
A power line is de-energised when the power company has cut the current in it. This is also called switching the line off.
Electric current flows in the line. A live line looks the same as a de-energised one.
The minimum distance from a hazard, such as a live power line, within which no one works and no water is directed.
The place from which the incident commander runs the incident and keeps in contact with the units.
The person who leads the rescue operation on scene and decides the units' tasks.
A part of the fire or work area with its own name (e.g. L1). Dividing the area into sectors makes it easier to give tasks.
Higher command's instruction on the general way to act in the situation. The plan is made within it.
The place or task where most of the resources are concentrated.
A condition agreed in advance: when it is met, a sector leader may move their units to another task without asking command first.
In the plan: the way the main effort works, e.g. direct attack, a defensive line or protecting settlements.
Your plan of which sectors and tasks the crews and drones are assigned to.
Extra units called to the scene later.
An understanding of what is happening: where the fire and the units are, and how the situation is developing.
Moving people away from a dangerous area.
The emergency centre answers emergency calls (112) and alerts the units.
The regional authority responsible for fire prevention and rescue operations.
A fire brigade of trained volunteers that has an agreement with the rescue department.
A call sign is the name a unit is called by on the radio. Call signs starting with EK are units of the own rescue department; the number tells them apart.
A call sign. Call signs starting with KY are units of the neighbouring rescue department.
A call sign. Call signs starting with OUT are units coming from outside the region.
A call sign. Call signs starting with DR are the drone team's drones.
A fire engine with its crew: it carries a pump, hoses, firefighting equipment and some water.
The people of a unit. 1+4 means one leader and four others.
A fire vehicle whose main task is to carry a large amount of firefighting water, several cubic metres.
A unit equipped for wildfires: an off-road vehicle with a trailer or container carrying hoses, portable pumps and basins.
An uncrewed aircraft, remotely piloted or flying on its own. At wildfires, drones film the fire from above with an ordinary and a thermal camera.
A drone that takes off and lands vertically like a helicopter but flies on wings like a plane. It stays in the air longer than an ordinary multicopter.
A drone that carries water and drops it on the fire.
An uncrewed ground vehicle that lays hose across the terrain.
A helicopter that scoops water from a lake with a bucket and drops it on the fire.
A water container hanging under a helicopter or a drone, filled from a lake or river and emptied over the fire.
A small plane that flies over the area to find and follow wildfires and reports what it sees.
A camera that shows differences in temperature. It shows hot spots through smoke and in the dark.
The ground area a camera sees at one time.
A break in the radio link between a drone and its ground station. No images arrive during it.
The source's own rating of how certain its observation is (e.g. good or moderate). It can drop, e.g., with poor visibility or a link outage.
Data a device records automatically, e.g. a drone's altitude, position and battery charge.
A narrow, usually gravel road built for forestry transport.
A track in the forest made by forestry machines. It is not a proper road.
